newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zambia mining industry set for rebirth.
newsitem.headline: Zambia mining industry set for rebirth.

text.p: Zambia's struggling mining industry is set for a rebirth with the imminent privatisation of two of its biggest copper mines, analysts said on Wednesday.

A consortium led by mining giant Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd said on Wednesday it was prepared to buy a majority shareholding in Zambia's Konkola Deep copper mine on which it had agreed to conduct an exclusive feasibility study.
The Zambian government is also expected to make an announcement on the sale of Zambia Consolidated Copper Mines Ltd's (ZCCM) Konkola North copper operation within the next two or three days.

Investment analyst John Clemmow of stockbrokers Investec Ferguson Brothers said the Zambian mining industry was set for a renaissance with production set to surge over the next 15 years to more than a million tonnes of copper a year from around 380,000 at present.
"It is a real rebirth. It is a big thing and to my mind it is the biggest mining story of the year," Clemmow said.

"I think the turnaround of the industry is the privatisation of ZCCM of which this is a part. That (privatisation) is proceeding apace, within the next two to three days we will see an announcement of the sale of Konkola North to Avmin."
Avmin Ltd is the minerals division of South African mining house Anglovaal Ltd. Zambia's privatisation agency said last year the deal with Avmin should be signed this month.
The Zambian government has said the privatisation of ZCCM -- which accounts for about 90 percent of Zambia's foreign earnings -- would turn around the country's economy.

Development of the two Konkola mines is seen as crucial to the rehabilitation of the mining industry -- once one of the biggest producers of copper and cobalt in the world but now only the seventh-biggest producer of copper.

The Konkola Deep consortium is led by Anglo subsidiary Zambia Copper Investments Ltd (ZCI) and also includes South African mining house Gencor Ltd and Falconbridge Ltd. The group announced on Wednesday it had signed a memorandum of understanding with the Zambian government and ZCCM to conduct an exclusive study on the Konkola Deep project.

It said it would also be prepared to assume ownership of the majority shareholding in a company called KonkCo -- which will include the existing assets and operations of ZCCM's Konkola division and Mufulira smelter and refinery -- in the second half of 1997 prior to a final decision on the project.
Metals analyst Stephen Briggs of stockbroker E.W. Balderson said he expected the new Konkola Deep mine to be producing an annual 100,000 to 180,000 tonnes of copper in five years.
"You'd be looking at an absolute minimum of 100,000 tonnes a year which is a quarter of what Zambia currently produces. Obviously it makes a big difference," he said.
He said Konkola Deep was seen replacing output from ZCCM's flagship Nchanga open-pit mine which would run out of ore in the next two or three years.
"The only way that you would sustain Zambian production..is by replacing the Nchanga open pit with Konkola Deep," Briggs said.

Clemmow said he believed the privatisation of ZCCM's mines would attract far higher bids than originally thought and predicted future investment in mining projects in the country to be upwards of $1.5 billion to $2.0 billion.

"The indications that we have seen so far is that bids are going to be substantially higher than was anticipated. Most of the major mining companies in the world will be bidding for some very significant assets in which they are going to be putting a lot of money."
